rationale: B wins because it has the discipline to keep three real lanes: price, labor, and restaurant operations. It correctly calls "Autocado halves guac prep time" a proof point, not a separate story, while A pads the board with "In Chipotle's test kitchens, one robot cut guacamole prep time in half." A is sharper on the rollout skepticism, but B's "Chipotle says it won't raise prices this year, even as its food costs climb" is the cleaner reporter-shaped angle.
gaps_in_A: "In Chipotle's test kitchens, one robot cut guacamole prep time in half" is too thin as a standalone angle. That number belongs inside the operations or rollout story unless there is methodology, baseline time, and scale proof.

"Chipotle is automating both ends of the kitchen — not just the guac" overstates the record. The facts show one 100-restaurant deployment and one system in testing, not yet a proven kitchen-wide automation strategy.

"Autocado plus the in-testing Digital Makeline reads as a coordinated strategy" is plausible, but still a thesis in search of an executive rationale. It needs confirmation before it becomes a pitch spine.
gaps_in_B: "Food robotics has been stuck in pilot-program purgatory" is an unsupported industry claim. Good line, bad sourcing. Do not smuggle a trend into the room without evidence.
"100 stores is the pilot-to-deployment threshold this beat watches for" invents a threshold. Reporters hate fake precision dressed as beat wisdom.
"Restaurant robots leave the pilot phase" gets ahead of the safer story. With 100 of 3,500+ stores, the better tension is whether this is a real rollout or a pilot wearing nicer shoes.
"Next step: journalist-fit-check" is premature for the strongest claims. First nail down price-pledge terms, store-level labor evidence, and rollout timing; then shop names.
